query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small fraction (2–5 at%) of nickel (Ni) into HfZrTiTa0.53 via arc melting and homogenization will increase its tensile ductility and uniform elongation at room temperature under quasi-static tension, without significantly reducing yield strength or impact-triggered energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy, as previously reported with 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain.
generation.intervention: Add 2–5 atomic percent Ni to the base alloy, producing HfZrTiTa0.53Ni0.02–0.05, followed by arc melting, homogenization, and standard sample preparation.
generation.conditions: Room temperature (20–25°C), quasi-static tension (strain rate ~10^-3 s^-1), compression, and impact tests; samples must be fully dense and single-phase.
generation.structural_mediator: Ni addition promotes local chemical heterogeneity and may stabilize a more ductile solid-solution microstructure, reducing lattice distortion and facilitating dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Ni acts as a ductility-promoting element in refractory alloys, reducing stacking fault energy and enhancing dislocation mobility, thus increasing uniform elongation and tensile ductility without severely compromising strength or impact-triggered energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HfZrTiTa0.53, the Ni-modified alloy will show at least a 50% increase in uniform elongation and tensile ductility (terminal strain >20%), with yield strength retained within 10% of the baseline, and impact tests will show comparable or improved energy release.
generation.baseline: HfZrTiTa0.53: yield strength 786 MPa, compressive strength 1314 MPa, terminal strain 13.5%, as reported.
generation.boundary: Applicable to single-phase, fully dense HfZrTiTa0.53 alloys with Ni additions up to 5 at%, tested at room temperature under quasi-static loading; higher Ni content or elevated temperatures may alter phase stability or mechanical response.
generation.uncertainty: Lack of direct tensile data for Ni-modified HfZrTiTa0.53; effect size is estimated based on Ni's known role in other refractory alloys, but phase stability and energy release under impact may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfZrTiTa0.53Ni0.02–0.05 samples via arc melting and homogenization. Conduct room-temperature quasi-static tensile tests to measure yield strength, uniform elongation, and terminal strain. Perform matched compression tests and impact tests (thin-steel-target penetration) to assess energy release.
measurements: Impact energy release (J or comparable metric)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-modified alloy does not show at least a 50% increase in uniform elongation (terminal strain >20%) compared to baseline, or if yield strength decreases by more than 10%, or impact energy release is significantly reduced, the hypothesis is falsified.
